summary: Specifies how the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) can be used as an encryption algorithm in the User-based Security Model of SNMPv3. This gives network management messages a stronger privacy option than the older DES-based choice.

plainLanguage.summary: SNMPv3 hides the management information in a message from anyone who should not read it. This RFC describes how to do that with AES, the modern encryption standard, instead of the older DES-based method. It also explains where the encryption key comes from, how the starting value for each message is built, and why the encryption must always be paired with one of the security model's authentication protocols.

questions: how is the iv built in snmp usm aes
subtitle: How SNMPv3 encrypts the management information in a message with AES, and how the key and the starting vector are derived.

tldr.problem: The User-based Security Model for SNMPv3 shipped with a privacy protocol based on CBC-DES, an algorithm no longer considered strong. The security model allows other protocols, but any replacement has to work with the existing authentication protocols and message format.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines CFB128-AES-128: the AES cipher with a 128-bit key, used in cipher feedback mode with all 128 bits fed back. The first 128 bits of the localized key become the encryption key, and the initialization vector is built from the engine's boot count, its engine time and a 64-bit salt that travels in the message.
tldr.outcome: SNMPv3 gains a privacy protocol based on the AES standard, in a form that interoperates with the HMAC authentication protocols already defined for the security model. Because cipher feedback mode does not detect tampering, the RFC requires the protocol to be used with one of those authentication protocols.

today: RFC 3826 is a Proposed Standard from June 2004 and is neither obsoleted nor updated. It adds a privacy protocol to the User-based Security Model defined in RFC 3414, which is also where the authentication protocols it must be paired with are specified, and it registers the protocol with IANA under the registration point the SNMP architecture keeps for privacy protocols.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
Inside the architecture for describing Internet management frameworks, the User-based Security Model (USM) for SNMPv3 is defined as a security subsystem within an SNMP engine. The USM describes HMAC-MD5-96 and HMAC-SHA-96 as the initial authentication protocols and CBC-DES as the initial privacy protocol, but it allows other protocols to be used instead of, or concurrently with, those.

This memo describes the use of CFB128-AES-128 as an alternative privacy protocol for the USM. The main goal is to provide a new privacy protocol based on the Advanced Encryption Standard. The major constraint is to maintain complete interchangeability with the authentication and privacy protocols already defined in the USM, so that the new protocol can be deployed without changing anything else.

For a given user, the AES-based privacy protocol must be used with one of the authentication protocols defined in the USM specification, or with an algorithm providing equivalent functionality. A privacy protocol on its own hides the contents of a message but does not prove who sent it, and the mode of encryption used here does not detect a modified message either.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMPv3 has a security subsystem that can encrypt the management information inside a message. It started with an encryption protocol built on DES, an algorithm no longer considered strong. This RFC adds one built on AES, and the rule is that it has to be used with the authentication protocols the security model already defines.

sections.title: The MIB Module and the Registered Identifiers
sections.content:
The document defines a small MIB module, written in SMIv2, that carries the object identities needed to use AES within the User-based Security Model. The module is SNMP-USM-AES-MIB, and it is written in SMIv2 as the USM specification requires.

The module contains one module identity, snmpUsmAesMIB, whose description reads "Definitions of Object Identities needed for the use of AES by SNMP's User-based Security Model". It sits at OID 20 under the snmpModules subtree. Inside it is one object identity, usmAesCfb128Protocol, described as the CFB128-AES-128 Privacy Protocol, with references to the two NIST documents that specify AES and its modes of operation. It sits at OID 4 under the snmpPrivProtocols registration point defined in the SNMP architecture document.

Both assignments were made by IANA: OID 20 for the module under snmpModules, and OID 4 for the protocol under snmpPrivProtocols. The registry of SMI numbers is where the first of them is recorded.
sections.plainLanguage: Two names are registered with IANA so that software can refer to this protocol by number: one for the MIB module that describes it, and one for the protocol itself under the registration point where the architecture keeps its privacy protocols.

sections.title: Key Localization and Passwords
sections.content:
A localized key is a secret key shared between a user and one authoritative SNMP engine. Even though a user may have only one pair of authentication and privacy passwords, and therefore only one pair of keys, for the entire network, the actual secrets shared between the user and each authoritative SNMP engine are different. That is achieved by key localization, performed for the authentication protocols of the USM by the two-step process described in section 2.6 of that specification.

The security of a cryptographic function depends both on the strength of the function against attacks and, perhaps more importantly, on the keying material used with it. While theoretical attacks against the functions are possible, key guessing is the more probable main threat.

The RFC therefore recommends that a password be at least 12 octets long, that password sharing be prohibited so that passwords are not shared among multiple SNMP users, and that implementations support randomly generated passwords as a stronger form of security. It also matters where the secret is kept: if a user's password or a non-localized key is disclosed, key localization will not help and network security may be compromised. A user's password or non-localized key must therefore not be stored on a managed device. The localized key is stored instead, if it is stored at all, so that if one device is compromised no other managed or managing device is compromised with it.
sections.plainLanguage: The same user has a different secret at each engine, derived from one password, so that leaking one secret does not open the others. The password itself is never kept on the managed device, only the derived key, and it should be long, unshared and ideally random.

sections.title: The AES Parameters
sections.content:
AES is the symmetric cipher algorithm that NIST selected in a four-year competitive process as the replacement for DES. The mode of operation decides how the cipher is applied to a message of any length. NIST Special Publication 800-38A recommends five confidentiality modes for use with AES: Electronic Codebook (ECB), Cipher Block Chaining (CBC), Cipher Feedback (CFB), Output Feedback (OFB) and Counter (CTR).

The protocol described here uses AES in CFB mode with the parameter S, the number of bits fed back, set to 128, following the definition of CFB mode in that publication. This mode requires an initialization vector the same size as the block size of the cipher algorithm.

Three further parameters follow the recommendations of the same publication. AES is used with a key size of 128 bits. The block size of the cipher is 128 bits, which fixes the size of the initialization vector. The number of rounds, which determines how many times a block is encrypted, is 10.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol uses AES with a 128-bit key and a 128-bit block, in the mode called cipher feedback, where the whole block of output is fed back into the next round of encryption. The cipher runs 10 rounds.

sections.title: The Encryption Key and the Initialization Vector
sections.content:
The size of the localized key of an SNMP user depends on the authentication protocol defined for that user at the authoritative engine. The protocol in this memo must be used with an authentication protocol that generates a localized key of at least 128 bits, and the authentication protocols defined in the USM specification satisfy that requirement.

The first 128 bits of the localized key are used as the AES encryption key. The 128-bit initialization vector is obtained as the concatenation of the authoritative engine's 32-bit snmpEngineBoots, the engine's 32-bit snmpEngineTime, and a local 64-bit integer. The 32-bit boot count is converted to the first four octets, most significant byte first, the 32-bit engine time to the next four octets in the same way, and the 64-bit integer to the last eight octets.

The 64-bit integer is then put into the msgPrivacyParameters field, encoded as an OCTET STRING of length 8 octets, and it is modified for the next message. The RFC recommends incrementing it by one until it reaches its maximum value, at which point it wraps. An implementation may use any method to vary the value, provided the method never generates a duplicate initialization vector for the same key. A duplicate can arise in the very unlikely event that multiple managers talking to a single authoritative engine both pick the same 64-bit integer within a second.

Because the receiver has to compute the same initialization vector, the sender and the receiver must use the same values of the individual components. Both use the values of snmpEngineBoots and snmpEngineTime carried in the message, and the same 64-bit integer carried in privParameters. That 64-bit value is called the salt in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message gets its own starting value for the cipher. It is built from the engine's boot count, its current time value and a 64-bit number that the engine keeps changing. The 64-bit number is sent along with the message so the receiver can rebuild the same starting value and decrypt the text.

sections.title: Encrypting and Decrypting the Payload
sections.content:
The data to be encrypted is treated as a sequence of octets and encrypted in cipher feedback mode with the parameter s set to 128. The plaintext is divided into 128-bit blocks. The last block may have fewer than 128 bits, and no padding is required.

The first input block is the initialization vector, and the forward cipher operation is applied to it to produce the first output block. The first ciphertext block is produced by exclusive-ORing the first plaintext block with that first output block, and the ciphertext block is also used as the input block for the next forward cipher operation. The process is repeated with the successive input blocks until a ciphertext segment has been produced from every plaintext segment. The last ciphertext block is produced by exclusive-ORing the last plaintext segment of r bits, where r is less than or equal to 128, with the segment of the r most significant bits of the last output block.

Decryption runs the same way round. The initialization vector is the first input block, the first ciphertext is used for the second input block, the second ciphertext for the third, and so on. The forward cipher function is applied to each input block to produce the output blocks, and the output blocks are exclusive-ORed with the corresponding ciphertext blocks to recover the plaintext. The last ciphertext block, whose size is at most 128 bits, is exclusive-ORed with the segment of the r most significant bits of the last output block to recover the last plaintext block.
sections.plainLanguage: The text is encrypted a block at a time. Each block of cipher output is exclusive-ORed with the matching block of plain text, and the cipher output becomes the input to the next block, so each block depends on all the ones before it. The last block may be short and needs no padding. Decryption runs the same chain backwards.

sections.title: Processing Outgoing and Incoming Messages
sections.content:
For an outgoing message, the SNMP engine first uses the secret encryption key to construct the AES encryption key. It sets the privParameters field to the serialization of an OCTET STRING holding the 64-bit integer that will be used in the initialization vector. It then encrypts the scopedPDU and serializes the encrypted data as an OCTET STRING. The serialized OCTET STRING of the encrypted scopedPDU is returned together with the privParameters and a status indicating success.

For an incoming message, the engine checks the privParameters field first. If it is not an OCTET STRING of 8 octets, the engine returns a decryption error to the calling module. It then extracts the 64-bit integer from that field, and uses the secret decryption key together with the integer to construct the AES decryption key and the initialization vector. The encrypted PDU is decrypted, and if it cannot be decrypted the engine returns a decryption error. On success it returns the decrypted scopedPDU and a status indicating success.

The privacy key of a user is different at each authoritative SNMP engine, so the msgAuthoritativeEngineID carried in an authenticated message is used to select the right key. The caller selects the key and passes the localized secret key to the privacy module, and the module works only with that key.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending a message means building the key, recording the salt in the message, and encrypting the part that carries the management information. Receiving one means checking that the salt is the right size, rebuilding the same key and starting value, and decrypting.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of the cryptographic functions defined here lies both in the strength of the functions themselves against various forms of attack and, perhaps more importantly, in the keying material used with them. The recommendations on passwords in the introduction should be followed to give the passwords maximum entropy and to protect them while they are stored.

The security of the cipher feedback mode relies on using a unique initialization vector for each message encrypted with the same key. If the vector is not unique, a cryptanalyst can recover the corresponding plaintext. The procedure in this document derives the vector from a local 64-bit integer initialized to a pseudo-random value at boot time, and an implementation may use any method to vary that integer, provided it never generates a duplicate vector for the same key. The suggested method of incrementing the integer produces a unique vector for every message, and can only produce a duplicate in the very unlikely event that multiple managers talking to one authoritative engine both pick the same integer within a second.

This protocol must be used with one of the authentication protocols defined in the USM specification, or with an algorithm providing equivalent functionality including integrity, because cipher feedback mode does not detect modifications to the ciphertext. The reader is also pointed to that specification and to the documents describing the cipher algorithms themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things matter for safety: the password has to be strong and kept off the managed device, and every message must start from a different value, because a repeated value would let an attacker work out the plain text. The encryption also has to be paired with authentication, since this mode of operation does not notice a changed message.

fields.name: snmpEngineBoots
fields.desc: Boot count of the authoritative engine, most significant byte first.

fields.name: snmpEngineTime
fields.desc: Time value of the authoritative engine, most significant byte first.

fields.name: Salt
fields.desc: Local 64-bit integer, sent in the privParameters field so the receiver can rebuild the same vector.

items.title: Start from the vector
items.text: The first input block is the initialization vector, and the cipher is applied to it to give the first output block.

items.title: Mix in the plain text
items.text: The first ciphertext block is the first plaintext block exclusive-ORed with that first output block.

items.title: Feed the output back
items.text: The ciphertext block also becomes the input block for the next forward cipher operation, so each block depends on the ones before it.

items.title: No padding
items.text: The last block may have fewer than 128 bits, and the last plaintext segment is exclusive-ORed with the r most significant bits of the last output block.

viz.caption: THE TWO DIRECTIONS OF THE PROCEDURE

cells: The secret encryptKey is used to construct the AES encryption key
The secret decryptKey and the 64-bit integer construct the decryption key and the vector
Set to the serialized OCTET STRING of the 64-bit integer used in the vector
Must be an 8-octet OCTET STRING, or a decryption error is returned
The scopedPDU is encrypted and returned as an OCTET STRING
The encryptedPDU is decrypted, and a decryption error is returned if it cannot be

data.code:
statusInformation =              -- success or failure
  encryptData(
  IN    encryptKey               -- secret key for encryption
  IN    dataToEncrypt            -- data to encrypt (scopedPDU)
  OUT   encryptedData            -- encrypted data (encryptedPDU)
  OUT   privParameters           -- filled in by service provider
        )
